name: Neck stretches / chin tucks
lead: Chin tucks are a head-retraction exercise in which the chin is drawn straight back, without tilting the head down, to engage the deep neck flexors. Neck stretches and chin tucks are used in physical therapy for posture-related neck complaints and are discussed in looksmaxxing forums as a way to improve neck posture, with some users adding weighted neck curls.[1][2]

On looksmax.org, proponents say regular chin tucks make the neck look better in profile and, in their view, raise the hyoid bone area, reducing the look of a soft submental region. Some posters share before-and-after photos as evidence.[3][4]

Clinical sources describe strengthening the deep neck flexors, including longus colli, as part of the management of forward head posture and neck pain.[1][5] No published study located for this article has examined chin tucks for hyoid position, jawline definition or facial appearance.

paras: Wikipedia's article on forward head posture lists strengthening of the deep neck flexors, stretching of the upper trapezius and strengthening of the muscles that retract the neck among commonly recommended measures, noting that some of those claims need independent confirmation.[1] Wikipedia's neck pain article states that craniocervical flexion motor-control exercises are effective for non-specific chronic neck pain and that specific strengthening exercises may improve function and pain.[5]
No studies found on chin tucks or neck stretches for facial or jawline appearance. Research on related exercises concerns neck pain and function rather than aesthetics.[5]

Forum threads ask whether chin tucks and neck curls are "cope or real." In one, a respondent said they are worthwhile unless the person expects them to transform overall attractiveness, and another said they are the best exercises for the hyoid area.[3] A poster in another thread shared photos after adding weight to chin tucks and reported improved posture.[4] These are anecdotes; no controlled data accompany them.

lore.intro: On looksmax.org, chin tucks and neck curls are a recurring topic, often framed as a test of whether neck work produces visible change.[3][4]

claims.claim: Chin tucks and neck curls raise the hyoid area
claims.believers: Posters say these are the best exercises for improving the hyoid region and a tighter neck-to-chin look.[3][4]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined hyoid position or submental appearance after chin tuck training; clinical literature addresses deep neck flexor strengthening for pain and posture.[5]

claims.claim: Adding weight to chin tucks makes visible before-and-after changes
claims.believers: One poster reported photos showing a difference at the same weight and facial fat after weighted chin tucks.[4]
claims.experts: No controlled studies are available; photo differences can reflect posture, angle and lighting, and none have been studied in this context.[1]

claims.claim: Chin tucks correct forward head posture
claims.believers: Forum users describe improved posture after daily practice.[4]
claims.experts: Clinical sources list deep neck flexor strengthening among approaches to forward head posture and chronic neck pain, with some statements flagged as needing confirmation.[1][5]

card.summary: Deep neck flexor exercise used in physio for posture; forums claim it lifts the hyoid area, but no appearance studies exist.
card.aka: Chin tucks, neck curls, neck retraction
card.note: Posture and pain use has clinical support; appearance claims have not been studied.

quick.overview:
Chin tucks pull the chin straight back to engage the deep neck flexors, and weighted versions are called neck curls. Physical therapy sources use similar exercises for forward head posture and neck pain.

Looksmax.org users say they improve neck posture and raise the hyoid area. No studies have examined those appearance claims.
quick.mechanism: The movement retracts the head over the shoulders and activates deep flexors such as longus colli. Forum believers say stronger flexors change how the chin and neck meet; this mechanism for appearance has not been tested.
quick.risks: Gentle exercise is generally low risk, but users report neck pain in some threads, and added weight raises load on the cervical spine. People with existing neck conditions are typically advised by clinicians to get assessed first.
